passages.title: The Return of the Red Kite
paras: For anyone driving along the motorway between London and Oxford today, the sight of a large, rust-coloured bird of prey circling above the fields is unremarkable. Yet only a few decades ago, the red kite had vanished entirely from England. Its return is widely regarded as one of the most successful wildlife reintroductions in British history, and it offers useful lessons for conservationists working with other species.

In the Middle Ages, red kites were common in towns as well as in the countryside. They were valued as scavengers: by feeding on rubbish and dead animals in the streets, they helped to keep settlements clean, and for a time it was even an offence to harm them. Attitudes changed from the sixteenth century onwards, when laws encouraged people to kill birds and animals that were thought to threaten crops and livestock. Later, the rise of large shooting estates in the nineteenth century made matters worse. Gamekeepers, whose job was to protect young pheasants and grouse, saw all birds of prey as competitors and shot, trapped or poisoned them in large numbers.

By the end of the nineteenth century, the red kite had been wiped out in England and Scotland. A small population survived only in the remote valleys of central Wales, where a few local landowners and volunteers protected nests from egg collectors. Even there, numbers remained dangerously low for most of the twentieth century, partly, it is thought, because the Welsh birds produced relatively few young.

In 1989, conservation organisations began a programme to bring the species back to England and Scotland. Rather than taking birds from the fragile Welsh population, they collected young kites from nests in Spain, and later from Sweden, where the species was still relatively common. The birds were released at carefully chosen sites, including the Chiltern Hills north-west of London. Before release, each bird was kept for several weeks in a large cage, or aviary, so that it could become familiar with its new surroundings. Each was also fitted with a small radio transmitter, which allowed scientists to follow its movements.

The choice of the Chilterns was not accidental. The area combined open farmland, where the birds could search for food, with patches of woodland that provided safe places to nest. Equally important, there were relatively few shooting estates nearby, which reduced the risk of illegal persecution. The results exceeded expectations. Within a few years the released birds had begun to breed, and their offspring spread steadily outwards. Today, red kites are a familiar sight across much of southern England, and the total UK population is estimated to be in the thousands of breeding pairs.

Not every release site was as successful. In some parts of northern Scotland, kite numbers grew far more slowly than expected, and examinations of dead birds revealed that many had died from eating poisoned bait that had been put out illegally to kill foxes or crows. The contrast between regions shows that habitat alone is not enough: a reintroduction depends just as much on how local people behave.

The red kite's comeback has also created some unexpected problems. In certain villages, residents began putting out meat in their gardens to attract the birds, and in some areas this has led to large groups of kites gathering over houses. Some people worry that the birds have become too dependent on human food, while others complain that kites occasionally snatch food from people's hands. Conservationists generally advise against feeding the birds, pointing out that there is plenty of natural food in the countryside.

Nevertheless, the project is now used as a model elsewhere. Supporters argue that its success came from three things: long-term funding, careful scientific monitoring and, above all, the support of farmers and landowners, who were consulted from the very beginning. Without that support, they say, even the best-planned release would have failed.

passages.title: The Box That Changed the World
paras: For most of history, loading a ship was a slow, labour-intensive business. Goods arrived at the docks in sacks, barrels, crates and bundles of every shape and size, and each item had to be lifted on board by teams of dock workers, known in Britain as dockers and in the United States as longshoremen. Fitting thousands of differently shaped objects into a ship's hold was a skilled job, and it could take longer to load and unload a vessel than to sail it across an ocean. Damage was common, and so was theft: dock work had a reputation for goods going missing somewhere between the ship and the warehouse.

The man usually credited with changing this was Malcom McLean, an American who owned a large trucking company rather than a shipping line. According to a story he often told, the idea came to him while he sat in his truck at a port in the 1930s, waiting for hours while his cargo was moved onto a ship piece by piece. Why, he wondered, could the whole trailer not simply be lifted on board? Two decades later he put the idea into practice. In April 1956, a converted oil tanker called the Ideal-X sailed from Newark, New Jersey, to Houston, Texas, carrying 58 metal containers on its deck.

The economic effects were immediate. McLean calculated that loading cargo in the traditional way cost around $5.86 per ton, while loading the Ideal-X had cost less than 16 cents per ton. Because containers could be packed at the factory and sealed, they also reduced theft and damage, which in turn lowered insurance costs. Ships spent days rather than weeks in port, which meant that each vessel could make more voyages a year.

Not everyone welcomed the change. For dock workers, containerisation threatened the jobs on which whole communities depended. A task that had once required a gang of twenty men could now be done by a single crane operator. Unions in several countries organised strikes, and in some ports long negotiations were needed before agreements were reached that protected the incomes of existing workers, even though fewer new workers would be hired.

A further obstacle was technical. In the early years, each shipping company designed its own containers, and the boxes of one company often could not be stacked on the ships, lorries or trains of another. A container that suited one firm's equipment might be a few inches too long for its rival's. It was not until the late 1960s that international standards for container sizes and corner fittings were agreed, allowing any box to be handled at any port in the world. The 20-foot container became the basic unit of measurement for the industry, and the capacity of ships is still expressed in 'twenty-foot equivalent units'.

Once standardisation was in place, the container transformed world trade. Because transport became so cheap, it was no longer necessary for factories to be close to their customers. Manufacturers could buy parts from one country, assemble them in another and sell the finished products on a third continent. Some economists now argue that the container did more to encourage globalisation than all the trade agreements signed in the same period.

The new system also had less visible consequences. Container ports need vast areas of flat land for storing boxes and deep water for giant ships, so cargo handling moved away from the old harbours in city centres to new sites, often many miles away. In cities such as London and New York, the traditional docks closed, and the neighbourhoods around them lost their main source of employment. Some of these areas were later redeveloped as offices and expensive housing, but for many former dock workers the change came too late.

passages.title: The Value of Boredom
paras: Boredom has a poor reputation. Parents try to protect children from it, employers see it as a threat to productivity, and an entire industry of apps, streaming services and games competes to make sure that we never have to experience it. Yet in recent years a number of psychologists have begun to argue that boredom is not simply an unpleasant state to be avoided. Some go further, suggesting that it may perform a useful function – and that our increasing ability to escape it could be doing us harm.

Part of the difficulty in studying boredom is defining it. Researchers generally agree that it involves a desire to be engaged in some satisfying activity combined with an inability to find one. This distinguishes it from relaxation, in which a person is content to do nothing, and from apathy, in which the desire to act is itself missing. Boredom, in other words, is not a lack of feeling but an uncomfortable state of wanting – and, like hunger or pain, it may exist to push us towards a change of behaviour.

How strongly people wish to avoid that discomfort was shown in a well-known series of experiments published in 2014. Participants were asked to sit alone in a plain room for between six and fifteen minutes with nothing to do but think. Many found the experience unpleasant. More strikingly, when given the option of pressing a button that delivered a mild electric shock, a considerable number chose to shock themselves rather than simply sit with their thoughts – even though, earlier in the study, they had said they would pay money to avoid such a shock. Men were considerably more likely than women to press the button.

If boredom is so unwelcome, what might be its value? One answer comes from research on creativity. In a study carried out in Britain, one group of volunteers was given a deliberately dull task – copying numbers out of a telephone directory – before being asked to think of as many uses as possible for a pair of plastic cups. A second group went straight to the creative task. The volunteers who had been bored first produced more ideas, and the effect was even stronger for a third group who had only read the numbers rather than copying them. The researchers suggested that boredom encourages the mind to wander, and that daydreaming allows unusual connections to be made.

This explanation fits with a broader body of work on what is sometimes called the 'default mode' of the brain, a pattern of activity that appears when a person is not focused on the outside world. During these periods, the brain is far from idle: it seems to be reviewing memories, imagining the future and making sense of experience. If every quiet moment is immediately filled with a phone or a screen, the argument goes, this kind of internal processing is crowded out.

It would be a mistake, however, to conclude that boredom is always beneficial. Chronic boredom – a frequent, long-lasting tendency to feel bored – has been linked to a range of problems, including poor performance at school, overeating and risky behaviour. In such cases, boredom seems less a spur to creativity than a sign that something in a person's life or environment needs to change. Nor does the creativity research show that bored people produce better ideas, only more of them; whether those ideas are useful is a separate question.

In my view, the most reasonable conclusion lies somewhere between the extremes. The occasional experience of boredom is not a problem to be solved but a signal worth listening to. When we feel bored, we are being told that our current activity is not meeting our needs. The healthy response is neither to suffer in silence nor to reach automatically for distraction, but to ask what we actually want to be doing. Children, in particular, may benefit from being left to find their own entertainment from time to time, since learning to cope with empty time is itself a skill.

What seems clear is that the technology which allows us to avoid boredom so easily has arrived far faster than our understanding of its effects. It would be foolish to blame smartphones for every modern problem. But it would be equally foolish to assume that a mind which is never allowed to be bored loses nothing in the process.

passages.title: The Humble Pencil
paras: Few objects are as ordinary as the pencil. It is cheap, light and reliable, and it works in conditions where pens fail – upside down, in freezing temperatures, even underwater. Yet the pencil has a surprisingly eventful history, involving shepherds, smugglers and a war between two of Europe's great powers.

The story begins in the sixteenth century in Borrowdale, a valley in the north-west of England, where a large deposit of unusually pure graphite was discovered. Local shepherds are said to have used lumps of the soft black mineral to mark their sheep. At the time, nobody understood what graphite was: because it left a grey mark like lead, it was called 'black lead', and the name has survived, even though modern pencils contain no lead at all.

Borrowdale graphite was so pure that it could simply be sawn into sticks and used for writing. It soon became extremely valuable, not only for artists and writers but also for industry, since it was used to line the moulds in which cannonballs were made. The English government took control of the mine, which was opened for only a few weeks each year to prevent prices from falling, and armed guards were employed to stop workers from smuggling graphite out of the valley.

Elsewhere in Europe, graphite was of poorer quality and broke easily, so pencil makers had to find other solutions. In Germany, craftsmen mixed powdered graphite with substances such as sulphur, but the results were disappointing. The decisive breakthrough came in France in 1795. Because of the war with Britain, French manufacturers could no longer obtain English graphite, and the government asked an engineer, Nicolas-Jacques Conté, to find an alternative. Conté mixed powdered graphite with clay, shaped the mixture into thin rods and baked them in a kiln. By changing the proportion of clay, he could make the pencil harder or softer – the basis of the grading system still used today.

Conté's method meant that good pencils could be made from low-quality graphite almost anywhere, and pencil making became a major industry, particularly in Germany and later in the United States. Wooden cases, which had previously been made by hand, began to be produced by machine in the nineteenth century, and the price of pencils fell dramatically.

The familiar yellow colour also has an interesting origin. In the late nineteenth century, some of the finest graphite came from Siberia, near the border with China. To advertise the quality of pencils made from it, one manufacturer is said to have painted them yellow, a colour associated with China. The idea was widely copied, and in North America yellow is still by far the most common colour for pencils.

In 1858, an American named Hymen Lipman was granted a patent for attaching an eraser to the end of a pencil. The idea was popular with customers, but the patent was later declared invalid by the courts, on the grounds that Lipman had simply combined two existing products rather than inventing something new. In many parts of Europe, pencils are still often sold without erasers.

Despite the arrival of computers and touchscreens, the pencil remains in heavy use. Billions are produced every year, and many artists, architects and students still prefer it, partly because mistakes can be corrected so easily. It is often claimed that a single ordinary pencil contains enough graphite to draw a line around fifty kilometres long.

passages.title: Cooling the City
paras: On a still summer evening, the centre of a large city can be several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside. This effect, known as the urban heat island, was first described in the early nineteenth century by Luke Howard, an amateur scientist who recorded temperatures in and around London. Today it is one of the best-documented features of urban climate, and as cities grow and summers become hotter, it is attracting increasing attention from planners and public health officials. Measurements in cities all over the world have since confirmed the pattern, and the difference tends to be largest in big, densely built cities.

Several factors combine to produce the effect. Dark surfaces such as asphalt roads and roofs absorb a large proportion of the sun's energy during the day and release it slowly at night, which is why the difference between city and countryside is usually greatest after sunset. Cities also have fewer trees and less open ground. In the countryside, plants release water vapour through their leaves, a process that cools the surrounding air in much the same way that sweating cools the human body. Finally, cities produce heat of their own, from vehicles, factories and, increasingly, air-conditioning units, which pump heat out of buildings and into the streets.

The shape of a city matters too. Where tall buildings line narrow streets, the heat given off by walls and pavements is trapped rather than escaping into the sky, and the buildings also reduce the wind that might otherwise carry warm air away. Researchers sometimes compare such streets to canyons. Paving over gardens and open land has a similar effect, since hard surfaces store heat and cannot release moisture into the air.

The consequences can be serious. During heatwaves, high night-time temperatures prevent people's bodies from recovering from the heat of the day, and older people and those with heart or breathing problems are particularly at risk. The European heatwave of 2003, which is estimated to have caused tens of thousands of deaths, prompted many governments to introduce warning systems and emergency plans. Higher temperatures also increase the demand for air conditioning, which raises energy use and, in a vicious circle, adds still more heat to the urban environment.

Fortunately, there are well-tested ways of reducing the problem. One of the simplest is to make roofs and roads lighter in colour, so that they reflect more sunlight. 'Cool roofs' coated with reflective paint can be many degrees cooler than conventional dark roofs on a sunny day, reducing the need for air conditioning in the rooms below. Green roofs, covered with plants, have a similar effect and also absorb rainwater, though they are more expensive to install and maintain. Some cities have also experimented with lighter-coloured pavements, although bright surfaces can cause uncomfortable glare and need regular cleaning if they are to stay reflective.

Trees are perhaps the most effective tool of all, since they provide shade as well as cooling the air through their leaves. However, planting trees in dense city centres is not as easy as it sounds. Underground pipes and cables leave little room for roots, and young trees need regular watering for several years. Some cities have therefore started to treat trees as part of their basic infrastructure, like roads and drains, with long-term budgets for their care rather than one-off planting campaigns.

passages.title: Is Earlier Always Better?
paras: It is widely believed that when it comes to learning a foreign language, the younger the better. Parents in many countries pay for English lessons for children who can barely read, and governments have moved the start of compulsory language teaching to ever earlier ages. The belief is not without foundation. But a closer look at the evidence suggests that the relationship between age and language learning is more complicated than the popular slogan implies.

The idea that there is a 'critical period' for language was popularised in the 1960s by the linguist Eric Lenneberg, who argued that the brain's ability to acquire language declines around puberty. Strong support seemed to come from a well-known study published in 1989, which tested the English grammar of Chinese and Korean speakers who had moved to the United States at different ages. Those who had arrived before the age of seven performed like native speakers; after that, performance declined steadily with age of arrival.

Crucially, however, the people in this study had learned English by immersion: they lived in the country where it was spoken and used it every day for years. That is very different from the situation of most children who learn a foreign language at school, where they may receive two or three hours of teaching a week. Studies of school learners tell a different story. A large research project in Spain, for example, compared students who had begun English at different ages in school. After the same number of hours of teaching, those who had started later, as teenagers, generally did better than those who had started as young children. Older learners, it seems, can make better use of limited input: they have more developed memories, can understand explicit explanations of grammar, and are better at using strategies such as taking notes.

Even in immersion settings, the advantage of youth is not equally strong in every area. It is most obvious in pronunciation, where those who start in early childhood are far more likely to end up sounding like native speakers. For vocabulary, by contrast, age of starting seems to matter much less, and adults often learn new words faster than children in the early stages.

None of this means that early teaching is a waste of time. Young children are often less anxious about making mistakes and more willing to imitate unfamiliar sounds, and an early start can give them a positive attitude towards other languages and cultures. But these benefits depend heavily on the quality of the teaching. If lessons are given by teachers who themselves lack confidence in the language, or if classes are large and children rarely get a chance to speak, an early start may achieve very little.

In my view, the debate has too often been framed as a simple question of age, when the more important factors are the amount and quality of the language that learners are exposed to. A twelve-year-old who has rich, frequent contact with a language will almost certainly overtake a six-year-old who hears it for an hour a week. Policymakers who move language lessons into primary schools without investing in teacher training are likely to be disappointed.

For adult learners, the research contains an encouraging message. While it is rare for people who start as adults to be mistaken for native speakers, many reach a very high level of proficiency, and some achieve near-native ability. Motivation, regular practice and opportunities to use the language seem to matter at least as much as the age at which one begins. 'Too late' is, for most practical purposes, a myth.

passages.title: Half Asleep
paras: For most of the twentieth century, scientists assumed that sleep was an all-or-nothing state: an animal was either awake, with its whole brain alert, or asleep, with its whole brain at rest. In the 1960s, however, researchers recording the brain activity of dolphins noticed something that did not fit this picture. While one half of the dolphin's brain showed the slow, regular waves typical of deep sleep, the other half remained fully awake. A few hours later, the two halves swapped roles.

This pattern, now known as unihemispheric slow-wave sleep, has since been found in many marine mammals and in a large number of birds. In each case, the eye connected to the waking half of the brain usually stays open, while the other eye closes. A sleeping dolphin can therefore keep watching its surroundings, and it can continue to swim slowly and rise to the surface to breathe. Unlike humans, dolphins do not breathe automatically; each breath is a deliberate action, so a fully unconscious dolphin would drown.

Birds appear to use half-brain sleep mainly for protection. In a well-known experiment published in 1999, researchers placed four mallard ducks in a row and filmed them as they slept. The two birds at the ends of the row spent far more time sleeping with one eye open than the birds in the middle, and they almost always kept the open eye pointed away from the group, towards the direction from which a predator would be most likely to come. When the end birds were moved to the middle, their behaviour changed within minutes.

The most remarkable evidence, though, comes from birds that sleep in the air. For decades it was suspected that frigatebirds, which can stay over the ocean for weeks at a time without landing, must sleep while flying, but nobody could prove it. In 2016 a team fitted small recording devices to the heads of fifteen frigatebirds in the Galapagos Islands. The data showed that the birds did indeed sleep in flight, sometimes with one half of the brain and sometimes with both, usually while gliding upwards on rising currents of warm air.

What surprised the researchers was how little the birds slept. On land, a frigatebird sleeps for more than twelve hours a day. In flight, the same birds slept for an average of only 42 minutes a day, in short periods lasting around twelve seconds each. How they manage to stay alert on so little sleep is still unknown, and it raises the question of whether the long hours that many animals spend sleeping are really as necessary as we think.

Humans cannot sleep with half a brain, but a milder version of the same effect may affect anyone who has spent a night in an unfamiliar place. Many people sleep badly on the first night in a hotel or a friend's house, a phenomenon that sleep researchers call the 'first-night effect'. In 2016, a study at Brown University found that during the first night in a sleep laboratory, the left half of the volunteers' brains slept less deeply than the right and responded more strongly to unusual sounds. On the second night, the difference disappeared.

The researchers suggest that this lighter sleep acts as a kind of night watchman, keeping part of the brain ready to wake the sleeper if something is wrong. The finding has a practical consequence for science itself: because the first night in a laboratory is unusual, many sleep studies now ignore the data from it and begin their measurements on the second night.

Half-brain sleep also raises questions that are not yet answered. If one half of the brain can rest while the other stays on guard, what exactly is being restored during sleep, and why do most animals, including humans, normally switch off both halves at once? Some scientists believe the answer lies in the high cost of keeping a whole brain awake; others think that some functions of sleep simply cannot be carried out by one half alone. Either way, the dolphins and frigatebirds suggest that sleep is far more flexible than was once believed.

passages.title: The Science of Waiting in Line
paras: Few everyday experiences are as universally disliked as waiting in a queue. Surveys in several countries suggest that the average adult spends the equivalent of several days a year standing in lines, whether at supermarket checkouts, airport security or the doctor's surgery. Yet the frustration people feel has surprisingly little to do with the actual length of the wait. A queue that lasts ten minutes can feel perfectly acceptable on one occasion and unbearable on another, and the businesses that manage queues best are the ones that understand why this happens.

One of the first people to study this question seriously was the American researcher David Maister, who in 1985 set out a number of principles of the psychology of waiting. The most famous of these is that unoccupied time feels longer than occupied time. Maister described a hotel in which guests constantly complained about slow lifts. Rather than install faster lifts, which would have been very expensive, the managers put mirrors next to the lift doors. The complaints almost stopped, because people waiting for the lift now had something to look at: themselves.

A second principle concerns uncertainty. People find a wait much easier to accept when they know how long it will last. This is why many theme parks display estimated waiting times at the start of each queue, and why some parks deliberately overestimate them. A visitor who is told to expect a forty-minute wait but reaches the front in thirty minutes feels pleased rather than annoyed, even though half an hour is still a long time to stand in the sun. An unexplained delay, by contrast, makes even a short wait feel endless.

Fairness matters too, often more than speed. In a study of supermarket shoppers, researchers found that customers were more irritated by seeing someone who had arrived later being served first than by the length of the queue itself. For this reason, many banks and post offices have replaced several parallel lines with a single 'serpentine' queue that feeds all the counters. On average, a single queue is not much faster, but it guarantees that people are served in the order in which they arrived, and customers consistently rate it as better.

The mathematics of queues is a field of its own, known as queueing theory, which began in 1909 with the work of the Danish engineer Agner Krarup Erlang on telephone exchanges. One of its most important findings is that waiting times do not increase steadily as a system gets busier. When a service is working at around half its capacity, queues are short; but as it approaches full capacity, the average wait rises extremely quickly. A checkout that is busy 95 per cent of the time will have far longer queues than one that is busy 85 per cent of the time, even though the difference in workload is small.

Technology is now changing the experience of waiting altogether. Many restaurants and clinics send a text message when it is a customer's turn, allowing people to wait somewhere more comfortable, and some airports show live waiting times for security on their websites. Such systems do not make the wait itself any shorter, but they turn empty time into free time that people can use as they like. If Maister's principles are correct, that may turn out to be the most effective improvement of all.

passages.title: Can Machines Translate Poetry?
paras: When the first computer translation systems were demonstrated in the 1950s, their creators predicted that the problem of translation would be solved within a few years. It took rather longer. For decades, machine translation produced text that was understandable at best and ridiculous at worst. In the last ten years, however, systems based on neural networks have improved so dramatically that, for many everyday purposes, their output is now difficult to distinguish from the work of a competent human translator. It is natural to ask whether there is anything left that machines cannot do.

Poetry is often offered as the obvious answer, and I think the claim deserves more careful examination than it usually receives. Those who make it tend to argue that poetry depends on qualities that cannot be reduced to rules: sound, rhythm, ambiguity and the associations that words carry for a particular culture. A machine, they say, translates meaning, and a poem is more than its meaning. There is something in this argument, but it is weaker than it first appears, because it assumes that human translators succeed where machines fail. Often they do not.

Translators of poetry have always disagreed about what a good translation is. Some believe that the translator's first duty is to the literal sense of the original; others argue that a poem should be recreated as a poem in the new language, even if this means changing its images or its argument. The Russian-American novelist Vladimir Nabokov famously insisted that the only honest translation of Pushkin's verse novel Eugene Onegin was a literal one, and produced a version so faithful that many readers found it almost unreadable. His critics produced versions that rhymed beautifully but said things Pushkin had never said.

If skilled human beings cannot agree on what success looks like, it is hard to claim that machines have clearly failed. In a small experiment carried out at a European university in 2021, readers were shown pairs of translations of short poems, one by a professional translator and one by a machine, without being told which was which. When asked which they preferred, the readers chose the human version only slightly more often than the machine version. When asked to identify the human translation, they did little better than chance.

None of this means that machines are good poets. What the experiment shows, I would argue, is that readers judge translated poetry largely on whether it reads naturally, and modern systems are extremely good at producing natural-sounding text. They are much less good at the decisions that make a translation interesting: when to keep a strange image, when to sacrifice a rhyme, when to leave an ambiguity unresolved. These are choices, and a machine does not make choices in the way that a translator does; it selects the most probable option.

That difference matters most for the poems that matter most. A great poem is rarely the most probable arrangement of its words; it surprises us. A system trained to produce likely sentences will tend to smooth out exactly the features that make the original unusual, and the result may be fluent but flat. Several translators who have tested these systems report the same experience: the machine version is a useful first draft, but the real work begins when they start to disagree with it.

The future of poetry translation is therefore likely to be neither purely human nor purely mechanical. Already, many professional translators use machine output to check their understanding of a difficult line or to see options they had not considered. Some readers will regret this. I do not. A tool that makes the translator's choices more visible, rather than making them for her, could make translation a more thoughtful art, not a less human one.
